howItWorks.intro: Diesel cost per mile starts as a burn-rate calculation, not a full ownership calculation: price per gallon ÷ miles per gallon gives you the fuel cost of moving one mile forward. From there the calculator multiplies that figure by your daily miles, then scales it into weekly, monthly, and annual totals using the days-per-week you report — the number a dispatcher needs when pricing a lane, or a fleet manager needs when diesel jumps 30 cents overnight and the whole budget has to move with it.
rules: Cost per mile = diesel price / MPG
Daily cost = cost per mile × daily miles
howItWorks.outro: Two diesel-specific costs sit outside this formula and deserve their own line in your budget: diesel exhaust fluid (DEF), which most modern trucks consume at roughly 2-3% of diesel volume and adds about $0.01-0.02 per mile, and the extra fuel burned during automatic diesel particulate filter (DPF) regeneration cycles, which can add another 1-2% to consumption on trucks that idle heavily or run short, stop-and-go routes.

faq.question: What's the average MPG for a semi truck?
faq.answer: A loaded Class 8 semi truck averages 5.5-6.5 MPG. Empty trucks can achieve 7-8 MPG. Newer aerodynamic models may reach 8-10 MPG.

faq.question: How does diesel price affect shipping costs?
faq.answer: Fuel is typically 30-40% of trucking operating costs. A $1/gallon increase in diesel adds roughly $0.15 per mile, or about $70-80 per day for a long-haul trucker.

faq.question: Why does diesel usually cost more than gasoline?
faq.answer: Diesel carries a higher federal excise tax (24.4 cents/gallon vs. 18.4 cents for gasoline), refiners switch to costlier winter-blend diesel every fall to prevent gelling in cold weather, and diesel competes globally with heating oil and jet fuel for the same distillate barrel. A cold snap in Europe or a spike in export demand can push U.S. diesel prices up even while gasoline holds steady — the two fuels have traded places on which costs more several times in the past decade.

faq.question: How accurate is this calculator?
faq.answer: It gives you the diesel burn rate only — price per gallon divided by MPG, scaled to your daily, weekly, monthly, and annual mileage. It doesn't capture DEF consumption, DPF regeneration fuel, idle time, tires, or maintenance, so treat the result as your fuel line item and add those costs separately when you need a full per-mile operating figure.

faq.question: Which diesel price should I use — cash, credit, or fleet card rate?
faq.answer: Use whatever you actually pay at the pump you fuel at most. Truck stops routinely post a cash price, a higher credit-card price, and a separate (often lower) fleet-card or discount-network rate that can differ by $0.05-0.15 a gallon. If you fuel across multiple states, run this calculator with your average price paid over the last few fill-ups rather than the price posted at any single station, since diesel varies more state-to-state than gasoline does.

faq.question: Does winter diesel change my cost per mile?
faq.answer: Yes. Cold-climate stations blend in kerosene (creating a No. 1/No. 2 blend) to keep diesel from gelling below freezing, which typically adds $0.10-0.20 per gallon and slightly lowers energy content and fuel economy. Idling for cab heat or block-heater use on cold mornings burns fuel without adding miles, so a truck's real winter cost per mile often runs higher than the same route driven in summer, even at an identical MPG entry.

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Measures
sections.body: This tool isolates one number: the diesel burn rate per mile, found by dividing your price per gallon by your vehicle's fuel economy. That is not the same as a full operating cost per mile — it leaves out DEF, tires, maintenance, insurance, and truck payments, all of which belong in a broader calculation like our general Cost Per Mile Calculator. What you get here is the fuel line item isolated, which is exactly what a dispatcher needs when quoting a rate on short notice, or what a fleet manager needs the moment a regional diesel price jumps 30 cents overnight and every open load has to be re-priced before it books.

sections.title: Why Diesel Doesn't Move Like Gasoline
sections.body: Diesel and gasoline prices don't track each other the way most drivers assume. Diesel carries a higher federal excise tax (24.4 cents/gallon versus 18.4 cents for gasoline), refiners switch to costlier winter-blend diesel every fall to keep it from gelling in cold climates, and diesel competes globally with heating oil and jet fuel for the same distillate barrel — so a cold snap in Europe or a spike in export demand can push U.S. diesel prices up while gasoline holds steady. Diesel has traded both above and below gasoline in the same calendar year more than once in the past decade. The upside is energy density: a gallon of diesel holds about 11% more BTUs than a gallon of gasoline, and diesel engines run higher compression ratios, so a diesel pickup routinely beats its gasoline twin by 20-30% in MPG. That efficiency gap is what keeps diesel's real cost per mile competitive even when the pump price runs a dollar higher than gasoline.

sections.title: A Worked Example: Semi Truck vs. Diesel Pickup
sections.body: Run the numbers on a Class 8 sleeper at $4.10/gallon and 6.5 MPG: $4.10 ÷ 6.5 ≈ $0.631 per mile in diesel alone. At 500 miles a day, five days a week, that's $315.50 daily, about $1,577 weekly, and roughly $82,000 a year in fuel — before a single tire, oil change, or DEF top-off. Drop the same truck onto an empty-trailer backhaul at 7.8 MPG and the per-mile cost falls to $0.526, a reminder that the headhaul and backhaul legs of a round trip almost never cost the same to run. Now compare a 3/4-ton diesel pickup averaging 18 MPG on that same $4.10 diesel: $0.228 per mile, versus roughly $0.254 per mile for its gas-engine twin at 14 MPG and $3.55/gallon for regular. The diesel pickup costs more to buy and more to service, but it wins on fuel alone by about 2.6 cents a mile — real money over 15,000 annual miles, though nowhere close to enough to offset a semi's fuel bill, which dwarfs every other line item in a trucking budget.

howToSteps.title: Enter Today's Diesel Price ($/gal)
howToSteps.description: Pull the number from your fuel card statement or a current regional price index — diesel swings more from station to station and week to week than gasoline does, so a price from last week's fill-up may already be stale.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Vehicle's MPG
howToSteps.description: Use your actual logged average, not the sticker or manufacturer estimate. A loaded semi and an empty one can differ by 1-2 MPG, so pick the figure that matches the specific run you're pricing.

howToSteps.title: Set Daily Miles and Days Per Week
howToSteps.description: Enter the miles you actually cover in a driving day and how many days that pattern repeats, so the weekly and monthly totals reflect your real schedule instead of a generic five-day average.

howToSteps.title: Read the Weekly Through Annual Totals
howToSteps.description: Use the daily figure to price a single load, the weekly and monthly figures to check against a fuel budget, and the annual figure to see how much a price swing or a fuel-efficiency upgrade moves your bottom line over a full year.

tips: Diesel prices vary more by region and even by truck stop than gasoline does — check a current regional average rather than assuming last week's price still holds.
Loaded and empty legs rarely share an MPG number. Run the calculator once for your headhaul weight and again for the empty or partial backhaul to see the real spread.
Add DEF as a separate line item. It won't show up in the price-per-gallon field, but at 2-3% of diesel usage it's a real cost worth including in a rate quote.
Idle time is invisible to this calculator. A reefer unit or a truck idling overnight for cab climate control burns diesel without adding miles, so track idle hours against fuel receipts separately.

When comparing a diesel engine to its gas equivalent, run both at their actual logged MPG and current local pump prices — diesel's efficiency edge is usually 20-30%, not the flat assumption that diesel is simply cheaper to run.
